reference.source: Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: An X-linked peroxisomal disorder caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene, leading to accumulation of very-long-chain fatty acids in nervous tissue and the adrenal cortex
Presents across a wide phenotypic spectrum, from a rapidly progressive childhood cerebral form to the slower adult adrenomyeloneuropathy variant
The childhood cerebral form typically begins in a previously healthy boy with behavioural change, declining school performance, visual or auditory deficits, and progressive dementia and spasticity
Adrenomyeloneuropathy chiefly affects adult men with a slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, sphincter disturbance, and sensory loss reflecting distal axonopathy of long tracts

Adrenal insufficiency (Addison-like) may precede or accompany neurological disease, and some males present first with adrenal failure, so unexplained adrenal insufficiency in a boy or man should prompt VLCFA testing
Female carriers can develop a mild myelopathy in later life, so heterozygotes are not always asymptomatic
Elevated plasma very-long-chain fatty acids is the key biochemical screening test, confirmed by ABCD1 mutation analysis
The disorder is increasingly detected through newborn screening programmes, allowing presymptomatic identification and timely monitoring for cerebral disease and adrenal failure
There is no reliable phenotype-genotype correlation, so the same mutation within a family can produce very different clinical courses
reference.pathophysiology: Adrenoleukodystrophy results from loss-of-function mutations in ABCD1, which encodes a peroxisomal membrane transporter needed for the import and beta-oxidation of very-long-chain fatty acids. Impaired degradation leads to accumulation of these fatty acids in tissues, particularly cerebral white matter, spinal cord long tracts, adrenal cortex, and testis. In the cerebral form, an inflammatory demyelinating process destroys white matter, whereas adrenomyeloneuropathy is characterised by a slowly progressive distal axonopathy of the spinal cord. Adrenocortical cells accumulate abnormal lipid and undergo dysfunction, producing primary adrenal insufficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple sclerosis or other inflammatory demyelination
Hereditary spastic paraplegia (for the adrenomyeloneuropathy phenotype)
Subacute combined degeneration from vitamin B12 deficiency
Primary adrenal insufficiency of autoimmune or other cause
Attention/behavioural disorders in the early cerebral childhood form
additionalInvestigations: Plasma very-long-chain fatty acid profile as the principal screening test
ABCD1 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis and enable family testing
Brain MRI to detect and stage cerebral demyelination
Adrenal function assessment including morning cortisol and ACTH stimulation testing
Spinal cord imaging and nerve conduction studies in the adrenomyeloneuropathy phenotype
Newborn screening confirmation and genetic counselling for at-risk relatives
redFlags: A previously well boy with rapid cognitive, behavioural, or visual decline suggesting active cerebral demyelination
Unexplained primary adrenal insufficiency, especially with hyperpigmentation or adrenal crisis
Rapidly enhancing white matter lesions on MRI indicating an inflammatory, aggressive cerebral phase
Progressive gait failure with sphincter involvement in an adult male
reference.prognosis: The childhood cerebral form is often relentlessly progressive once inflammatory demyelination is established, whereas adrenomyeloneuropathy advances slowly over years to decades. Early identification through screening allows monitoring and consideration of disease-modifying options in appropriate candidates, and adrenal insufficiency can be effectively treated with hormone replacement, but neurological outcomes remain variable.
pitfalls: Attributing early cerebral disease in a boy to a behavioural or psychiatric disorder and delaying imaging
Overlooking coexisting adrenal insufficiency, which can be life-threatening if untreated
Assuming female carriers are always asymptomatic
Failing to offer genetic counselling and family screening once a proband is identified
